articles.title: Bluesky says its recent outage was caused by another DDoS attack
articles.summary: This is the latest large-scale DDoS attack to hit the social networking site this year.
articles.body:
Social networking site Bluesky says its recent day-long disruption was caused by a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that flooded the site with junk traffic. The social network confirmed the incident in a post on Monday, confirming the attack had taken place over the previous 24 hours.

“We have upgraded our defenses in response, and we continue to monitor the situation,” Bluesky said in a post , without disclosing any more details.

A spokesperson for Bluesky did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the attack.

DDoS attacks involve pummeling a website or server with large amounts of junk traffic with the aim of overloading its resources and knocking it offline. These kinds of attacks often rely on using large amounts of hijacked internet-connected devices — enlisted into a residential proxy network or a botnet — to harness their unused internet bandwidth to flood web servers.

Security researchers discussing the attacks in the IFIN public forum report that Iran-backed attackers have claimed responsibility for the attack. Iran has increased its attacks on U.S. businesses and critical infrastructure since the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war earlier this year.

This is the latest large-scale DDoS attack to affect the social networking site in recent months. In April, the site was hit by a prolonged series of outages caused by a similar flood of web traffic . It’s unclear if the attacks are linked.

articles.title: Comcast adds motion sensing to millions of its newer routers, with a privacy catch | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A new feature added to Comcast's newest routers can detect if there is motion inside your home without needing traditional motion sensors.
articles.body:
Comcast has rolled out a new motion-sensing technology to its latest home routers, allowing homeowners to receive notifications about activity detected inside their house while they are away.

The free feature, called Wi-Fi Motion , turns newer Xfinity gateways into motion sensors by detecting interruptions to the Wi-Fi signal of the wireless network and sends a notification through the Xfinity app.

As first reported by The Verge , the new Wi-Fi Motion feature works for advanced Xfinity gateways XB7 and newer models and is opt-in, which means users can choose whether to switch on the feature in the Xfinity app. As quoted by the publication, customers can use this feature for “motion detection in their home and for a basic level of security.”

There is a privacy trade-off. By enabling the feature, Comcast says it may disclose information generated from a customer’s use of Wi-Fi Motion to outside parties under a broad array of reasons — and Comcast says it doesn’t have to tell you.

“Comcast may disclose information generated by your Wi-Fi Motion to third parties without further notice to you in connection with any law enforcement investigation or proceeding, any dispute to which Comcast is a party, or pursuant to a court order or subpoena,” reads an Xfinity support page .

That’s something to consider before you switch on the feature, particularly if you’re privacy conscious.

articles.title: Apple squashes EU beef with new App Store rules
articles.summary: Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says resolves its disagreements with the European Commission.
articles.body: Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says will resolve its “disagreements with the Commission over business terms and alternative distribution.” As part of the changes, every developer that distributes apps will be moved to a single set of business terms, and digital transactions for apps distributed outside of the App Store will be subject to a Core Technology Commission fee of 5 percent. The new terms go into effect on October 1st. They will include a 26 percent commission for App Store apps that use Apple’s in-app purchase system, or a 20 percent fee for developers using alternate payment providers. Developers must also pay a 15 percent commission on purchases that link out of the app. Apple will reduce these rates for developers in the App Store Small Business Program, Mini Apps Partner Program, or Video Partner Program. With the new terms, developers can offer both in-app purchases and alternative payment systems in the EU. However, developers must maintain the payment options they choose for 12 months “to provide consistency and clarity for users,” Apple says. There’s also a 5 percent Core Technology Commission on digital transactions in apps distributed on third-party app stores and the web. Apple will no longer charge an initial acquisition fee, store services fee, or the Core Technology Fee, a €0.50 per download fee that applied to apps for each annual install over 1 million.  Web distribution is only available in the EU, Apple says, and the company has eligibility requirements in place for who can actually operate a third-party app marketplace over the web, like being a publicly traded company or having completed a financial audit from a “licensed accountant.” Apple changed its App Store rules last year to comply with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a set of rules regulating Big Tech. The company has remained critical of the regulations and was fined last year after the Commission found that its App Store “anti-steering” practices violated the DMA. Apple lost its bid to exclude the App Store and iOS from the DMA last month. Apple’s updates also include new child safety features for the EU. Kids apps in the App Store can’t have links to websites for finishing transactions, and Apple won’t let App Store apps link out to websites for a purchase if a user is under 13 years old. Users under 18 will have to get permission from a parent or guardian when trying to make a purchase using an alternative payment method inside an App Store app.

articles.title: CareCloud confirms 3.7M patients had their medical records stolen in data breach | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The cyberattack at CareCloud resulted in one of the largest reported data breaches in the U.S. healthcare industry this year.
articles.body:
Hackers have stolen the personal information and medical records of more than 3.75 million people in a data breach at health data giant CareCloud, the company has confirmed with federal regulators. The disclosure marks the first confirmation of the scale of the data breach, which is now confirmed to be the fifth-largest theft of health data in 2026 so far.

CareCloud detailed the March data breach in a filing with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on Monday. The number of affected victims was reportedly revised up in an update on Tuesday, though it’s unclear if the figure is expected to rise further.

The New Jersey-based tech company provides electronic medical record storage to tens of thousands of healthcare providers around the United States, consequently serving millions of patients. CareCloud handles a large amount of patient data and billing information on behalf of hospitals, doctor’s offices, and other medical practices.

CareCloud has not publicly commented on the cyberattack since it disclosed the breach in March , when it said hackers had accessed patients’ medical data stored in one of its cloud storage environments over six days. The company later said in data breach notifications that the hackers exfiltrated data from the company’s Amazon Web Services account and stole reams of patient data.

The stolen data includes patients’ names, postal addresses, Social Security numbers, and their medical and health information. The hackers also took government-issued identification numbers, such as passports and driver’s licenses, as well as banking and financial information.

CareCloud chief executive Stephen Snyder has not responded to multiple emails requesting information about the incident, including whether the company has paid the hackers; who, if anyone, is responsible for cybersecurity at the company; or if Snyder plans to resign following the incident.

The breach at CareCloud follows several sizable healthcare breaches confirmed this year.

Tech giant TriZetto confirmed in March that a 2024 data breach affected 3.4 million people’s data, and an as-yet-unspecified number of people had their data stolen during a July data breach at health tech billing software maker Craneware.

According to HHS’ running tally of healthcare data breaches, dental insurance giant DentaQuest has had the largest data breach this year so far, with at least 15 million people’s personal and health information being affected.

articles.title: T-Mobile ‘chopped a cable’ to expel Chinese hackers from its network
articles.summary: The U.S. phone provider escaped a large-scale breach of its network after identifying Chinese-backed hackers early on.
articles.body:
New reporting from Bloomberg revealed how cybersecurity staff at U.S. phone provider T-Mobile identified and expelled Chinese hackers from its network in 2024 during a spate of industry-wide intrusions by Beijing aimed at stealing customer data.

The hacks were carried out by a Chinese government-backed hacking group called Salt Typhoon . The campaign compromised hundreds of phone companies, internet giants, and data center providers with the goal of collecting phone records and information about senior U.S. government officials, including then-presidential candidates. Hacked companies included AT&T, Verizon , satellite phone network Viasat , and network infrastructure giants Charter and Windstream .

By and large, T-Mobile escaped a widescale breach of its network by catching the activity early — and resorted to physically cutting the cable to a compromised system, per Bloomberg.

The publication said T-Mobile’s cyber staff spent months looking for suspected hackers in its network without success. Eventually, the company found unusual behavior on one of its systems coming from another router belonging to a different telecom company, which T-Mobile did not name.

After identifying the breach, T-Mobile’s cybersecurity chief, Jeff Simon, told Bloomberg that he and three others drove to the data center nearby to its Bellevue, Washington headquarters, found the compromised system, pulled out a set of scissors, and snipped the cable connecting the box to the outside world.

When reached by TechCrunch, T-Mobile did not provide comment.

articles.title: Air Force major detained again for Capitol protest after Trump criticism
articles.summary: A U.S. service member who was arrested on the steps of the U.S. Capitol last month after he advocated for President Trump’s impeachment was detained again, a U.S. Air Force spokesperson confirmed Wednesday evening. U.S. Air Force Maj. Jason Watson was ordered into “pretrial confinement” on Tuesday, the spokesperson told The Hill. Watson’s attorney, Christopher…
articles.body:
A U.S. service member who was arrested on the steps of the U.S. Capitol last month after he advocated for President Trump’s impeachment was detained again, a U.S. Air Force spokesperson confirmed Wednesday evening.

U.S. Air Force Maj. Jason Watson was ordered into “pretrial confinement” on Tuesday, the spokesperson told The Hill.

Watson’s attorney, Christopher Mutimer, told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Wednesday evening that the service member was arrested on duty and taken to a county jail on Tuesday after Watson informed his chain of command that he would “no longer be wearing his uniform.”

Mutimer told CNN he had spoken with Watson and confirmed his client is “doing well.”

The attorney said Watson’s legal team was awaiting the government’s evidence in the case ahead of a detention hearing on Thursday, and the service member has not yet been informed of his charges.

Watson’s detainment follows a Monday interview he sat for with Burnett, during which he defended his decision to call for the impeachment of Trump and Vice President Vance on the Capitol steps in July. The service member was protesting the U.S. military’s actions against Venezuela, Cuba and Iran under the Trump administration at the time.

“We just have to be willing to accept that we can change what is happening in our country if we’re just willing to pay a price for it,” Watson told CNN on Monday. “So, all that I could do is ask myself what’s the highest price that I’m willing to pay?”

An Air Force spokesperson told The Hill the case against Watson is still “under investigation” and confirmed he had not been formally charged as of Wednesday evening.

“Military members are required to comply with the Uniform Code of Military Justice and all applicable regulations,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Based on probable cause to support allegations of continued misconduct, Maj. Watson was ordered into pretrial confinement on Aug. 18, 2026.”

Mutimer told CNN he expected charges tied to articles 88 and 92 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which cover “ contempt toward officials ” and “ failure to obey order or regulation ,” respectively.

“He is facing significant jail time possibly. He is facing discharge from the military,” the attorney told CNN. “Depending how the government wants to stack charges or bring charges against him, we could be looking at serious jail time.”

articles.title: Army grapples with higher cadet standards after yanking memo
articles.summary: The Army is eyeing new minimum academic standards for college students in the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC), but not without some internal drama. The service branch issued fresh standards earlier this month, only to pull them days later amid differing opinions and an apparent lack of consultation with some senior leaders. Under the withdrawn…
articles.body:
The Army is eyeing new minimum academic standards for college students in the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC), but not without some internal drama.

The service branch issued fresh standards earlier this month, only to pull them days later amid differing opinions and an apparent lack of consultation with some senior leaders.

Under the withdrawn standards, incoming ROTC cadets would have to meet one of three academic benchmarks: score a 20 on the ACT, a 1000 on the SAT or test in the 50th percentile on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery (ASVAB), a standardized test on science, math and language.

“The Army must cultivate intelligent and adaptive officers to build a lethal and ready Army prepared to deter, fight, and win our nation’s wars. The strength of our Officer Corps is the strength of our Army,” Jay Hurst, who formerly served as the assistant secretary of the Army for manpower and reserve affairs, wrote in an internal Aug. 5 memo, which was obtained by The Hill.

The Army requires enlisted soldiers to score 110 on the ASVAB “line scores” to participate in Officer Candidate School, which trains civilians and enlisted personnel to gain a commission as officers in the armed forces. Line scores are a combination of subtests in the ASVAB that qualify candidates for certain career tracks in the military.

No equivalent standards exist for cadets to contract into the Army Senior Reserve Officer Training Corps, (SROTC) Hurst said in the internal document. Two days after signing the memo, Hurst was confirmed by the Senate as the Pentagon comptroller .

The new requirement was set to take effect in January next year. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, all students seeking to contract into SROTC must get a 110 on the ASVAB or provide proof that they met or exceeded “prescribed scores” on the SAT and ACT, the internal document said.

“SROTC Cadets already under contract are excluded from this requirement. This policy will only apply to undergraduate students,” the memo’s text said, adding U.S. Army Cadet Command would revisit the standards annually.

The under secretary of the Army, Mike Obadal, said it requires “further staffing and analysis,” according to an internal Aug. 12 memo, which was reviewed by The Hill.

The New York Post reported on Friday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was angry that the memo was rescinded. Hegseth’s office referred The Hill to the Army.

The rescission prompted gripes among some defense officials, who privately argue the service branch should have minimum standards in line with Hegseth’s push to raise standards for military officers, which has also included a focus on fitness and grooming.

The Army indicated that imposing standards is not dead but would require more input from senior leadership.

“The Army is in lock-step with Secretary Hegseth and the President’s direction regarding military standards and readiness,” an Army spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill. “The Army is evaluating proposed changes to ROTC cadet standards for review by appropriate senior leaders and approval by the Secretary of the Army and the Acting Chief of Staff of the Army.”

When reached for comment, the U.S. Army Recruiting Command said it had nothing further to add.

Will Thibeau, an Army veteran and director of the American Military Project at the Claremont Institute’s Center for the American Way of Life, said it is a “really positive sign” the Army is “considering establishing modest minimum standards for standardized tests that reinforce existing ROTC evaluation metrics.”

“The minimum standards outlined in the now-rescinded policy are below national averages, and we should expect more from those who will lead Americans in military service. I take the Army at their word that the step to rescind those standards is a step to double-check the timing and specific metrics of the policy,” Thibeau told The Hill on Wednesday.

Privately, some within the Pentagon saw the confusion around the Aug. 5 memo as evidence of disorder within the service branch. But others said Army leadership was not clued in, noting that Hurst is a Hegseth ally.

Not all of the “right” Army leaders, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, were given a chance to weigh in on standards in the memo before it was issued, two U.S. officials familiar with deliberations who spoke on condition of anonymity told The Hill.

“Part of the discussion was if the standards were high enough,” one U.S. official said, adding there is a desire within the service branch to make standards more “stringent.”

Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who is close with Hegseth and is nominated to be the next Army chief of staff , was not satisfied with the standards outlined in the Aug. 5 memo, a second U.S. official told The Hill.

LaNeve’s spokesperson declined to comment and referred The Hill to the Army. Hurst, through a spokesperson, declined to comment, referring The Hill to the Army.

Backers of the Aug. 5 memo say cadets should show intellectual agility before becoming officers. Others question if ACTs and SATs are reliable measures to assess an officer’s future performance.

“The SAT has not historically been a measure that is predeterminative of officer performance, and would serve to exclude candidates that would benefit from Army training, and the Army would benefit from developing the talent,” a former senior defense official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told The Hill on Wednesday.

Students in ROTC, upon completion of the program, can become second lieutenants in the U.S. Army Reserve, Army National Guard and Army.

Current Army rules already include academic, physical and other requirements. To secure an Army ROTC scholarship, applicants need to meet physical standards, have a minimum of a 2.5 unweighted high school GPA and take the SAT or ACT, but no minimum score is required.

But most cadets are not on scholarships, and the new standards would cover all Army SROTC enrollees. In 2024, just over a third of ROTC cadets were on scholarships.

articles.title: Meta glasses are a workplace menace
articles.summary: Meta glasses are quickly becoming a problem in workplaces. Public-facing workers are being filmed, harassed, and creeped out by AI-powered smart glasses.
articles.body: In August, Toru Hinkle was stocking shelves at their job at Target when they noticed two customers and asked if they needed any help. The men requested a price check on an item — but even after Hinkle told them the item was $20, the customers asked for the price again and again.  “After a while, I realized that I’m basically being pranked, and I noticed the glasses,” Hinkle says, referring to the frames with a blinking light. They were the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and the customers were filming. Hinkle eventually called a store manager over, but the pranksters antagonized her, too — asking the price repeatedly, deliberately misgendering Hinkle as “ma’am” and the female manager as “sir.” At one point, Hinkle attempted to stop the recording by saying “Meta, stop recording” out loud, hoping to trigger a voice control setting. The customers pretended to be confused by the accusation that they were recording Hinkle. The confrontation made Hinkle queasy. “I felt like this pit in my stomach just started to build up,” Hinkle recalls. “After this whole exchange happened, the rest of the shift, I was just quiet and didn’t even talk to anyone because I was just so shaken up by it.” Another customer called the police, Hinkle says, and the two men were escorted out of the store. Target declined to comment. The two customers were, in fact, recording Hinkle, and the entire exchange was turned into content for social media. Another Target manager came across the video while scrolling online, without even looking for it. One clip featuring the incident with Hinkle viewed by The Verge had almost 400,000 views on Instagram and 155,000 views on TikTok. Meta has sold millions of pairs of its AI-powered smart glasses over the last several years — but as sales boom, so too has the backlash to the devices. The glasses allow wearers to listen to music or take calls, but the feature that has sparked outrage is the ability to record using them: Many people see them as a new notch in the surveillance apparatus at best, and “pervert” and “creep” glasses at worst.  Ordinarily, if you are recorded against your will, you can try to leave the area or otherwise resist being recorded. But many people are encountering smart glasses for the first time while at their job, especially those who interact with the public, like retail and service workers. In the workplace, smart glasses exacerbate the power imbalance between the customer and the employee, or the boss and subordinate. Resisting invasive technology is risky when you depend on your job to pay rent or buy groceries. It’s harder still when many workplaces don’t yet have policies around a new gadget that the public is grappling with in real time. Service and retail workers in particular have become a target for stealth — and annoying — smart glasses recording. People wearing Meta glasses are going into stores and harassing or “pranking” employees, using the footage for content and making unwitting workers the butt of the joke. The video made of Hinkle and their manager without their consent is the exact kind of content that Instagram has claimed it will now remove — yet the account that uploaded it was filled with similar “prank” videos harassing workers at their jobs.  There’s little recourse for those who have been unknowingly recorded. In one of the videos posted to social media that Hinkle is featured in, the Meta glasses wearer is seen chumming it up and dancing with a police officer who arrived at the Target store. “You boys stay out of trouble,” the cop says as he fist bumps the person recording. Instagram banned the account — and along with it, removed the video of Hinkle — after The Verge asked the company about it. Emily, who works at a popular Seattle tourist destination, deals with vlogger questions and videographers trying to get close-up shots of the food her attraction sells. As a worker in an area with lots of foot traffic, being in the background of a video was just part of the job. More recently, though, the encounters have left her feeling deeply uncomfortable. The worst is when a much taller man stands over her and films her with his Meta glasses. She thinks — hopes — he is not filming down her shirt. But that’s what it feels like. “If someone was [holding] a phone up from that angle, I could obviously be like, ‘Hey man, please stop that,’” Emily says. The glasses make it much harder to tell what, exactly, a customer is filming. (Emily asked that The Verge only use her first name and not name her workplace, citing concerns of getting targeted.) Emily works as a cashier and interacts with up to 2,000 people a day. Even before Meta released its AI-powered smart glasses, people from all over the world visited and recorded videos at Emily’s workplace. But the new method of filming has quickly become part of her daily working environment: On some days, she says up to 10 people an hour will come in wearing smart glasses. The most preferable situation is that a customer filming her will use the video for relatively innocuous purposes, like a travel vlog or a food review. [Image: Satirical posters were plastered in New York protesting Meta glasses. “Worst-case scenario, they’re doing something significantly more nefarious with it,” Emily worries. “That is what’s significantly more scary to me … That feels like it’s a very easy way to get content of young women specifically.” Many of the encounters filmed using Meta glasses are explicitly gendered, like a genre of videos where men approach women with pickup lines and make content out of the encounters. Meta glasses have a light that indicates when they’re recording, but some people have tampered with the glasses to secretly record without being noticed. Meta says it is working on disabling filming capabilities if the glasses detect the light has been damaged or covered.  Emily is conscious of the fact that she’s a young woman working in a public place all the time, which adds to the baseline discomfort she feels. “I also want to emphasise how creepy I think the general surveillance aspect of it is, not just as a young woman, but as a person living [among] other people,” she says. “It does add to the feeling of constantly being watched.” Meta has maintained that privacy features are built into its smart glasses. “People use our glasses because they’re genuinely helpful – from listening to music, to live translation or hands-free calls. For those wearing them and the people around them, trust matters. That’s why we built privacy into our AI glasses from the ground up,” Meta spokesperson Dina El-Kassaby said in an email. El-Kassaby pointed to the LED indicator light that blinks when a user is taking a photo or video, and the tamper-proofing the company has started to roll out. El-Kassaby said Meta has begun blocking hashtags on its platforms associated with harassing content, including “rizz,” “pickup artist,” and “cold approach,” and has removed thousands of pieces of content under its bullying and harassment policy. The same rules apply to content filmed on other devices, like a smartphone, El-Kassaby says. But for years, the contemporary social media ecosystem has depended on strangers unwittingly becoming content — everything from this new wave of Meta glasses-powered “pranks” to people-of-Walmart-style gawking. A social internet cleansed of all content that takes advantage of others would be quite empty. For the first few weeks, Jennifer didn’t think much of her new boss. Then one day, he was wearing a different pair of glasses at their job at a Sprouts grocery store in the Atlanta area. She looked at him and asked, “Are those Meta glasses?” “Yeah, they are,” he said. “What of it?” Jennifer recalls starting to shake because their presence — and her boss’s lack of concern about how violating a recording device in the workplace could be — was so disconcerting.  Sprouts workers are barred from wearing headphones on the store floor because it’s a safety hazard when operating heavy machinery, Jennifer says, and non-managers are not allowed to have their phones with them. (She asked that The Verge use a pseudonym so she could discuss her experience freely.) What’s more, Jennifer says Sprouts stores prohibit videography and photography inside — customers who come in know the store has security cameras, but are likely not expecting employees to have glasses with built-in cameras in them, too. An employee wearing Meta glasses could break that trust with customers. Store employees also handle sensitive data at their jobs, including customers’ names, email addresses, and credit card information. Jennifer imagines her manager wearing Meta glasses in the break room, or the bathroom — places where a worker expects a certain level of privacy. “It essentially collapses the social contract, in my opinion, to allow this,” she says. Jennifer also worries that women and children shopping in the store are particularly endangered by the technology, and noted that the recording light on her boss’s glasses looked like it had been obscured in some way. Jennifer told The Verge that she filed a complaint to HR and asked that Sprouts make a formal policy around smart glasses, but found the company to be largely unresponsive and unhelpful. Instead, she says, she was given an ultimatum: Accept the working conditions or quit. She resigned.  “The issue is about the data that is collected, the footage, the audio, and the facial recognition that can be added to these glasses,” Jennifer says. “I want it so that it’s not acceptable for anybody to be doing that in the workplace.” Sprouts didn’t respond to The Verge’s requests for comment. Spy-like smart glasses are no longer a distant sci-fi future; they’re here now, and more tech companies are reportedly developing them. Workers, meanwhile, are left in the lurch as laws and company policies catch up to their daily reality. Experts say laws governing privacy in the US are scattershot, state-dependent, and often outdated. Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University, says information privacy law generally states that if you are in public, you have a reduced expectation of privacy — though some instances, like recording someone in a locker room changing, could open up the person recording to liability.  Workplace protections around being recorded, though, are almost entirely governed by corporate policy. Some workplaces have explicitly banned smart glasses: In August, Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced a policy that bars its employees from wearing Meta glasses because of the potential of capturing sensitive information. Some courthouses have also restricted smart glasses because they could be used to do things like identify jurors.  “The best hope for employees is through collective bargaining and policy-level rules around what kinds of recording technologies will be allowed and when they’ll be allowed to be used,” Hartzog says. Having smart glasses in the workplace could also create new liabilities for corporations that permit the devices: Businesses are charged with being stewards of customer and employee data, and as surveillance increases, so will the amount of abuses and breaches that accompany that surveillance, Hartzog says. He recommends strong and clear policies prohibiting the use of smart glasses — for both employees’ and customers’ sake. “We know that when people are being watched, they feel less free. They chill their behavior, they feel pressure to conform. They worry about even minor deviations from norms being used against them,” he says. “It’s just a sort of suffocating atmosphere to be a part of.” It’s not just service and retail workers who have come face-to-face with unwanted recordings while they’re working — creatives and performers are also grappling with a strange new reality. Earlier this summer, comedian Electra Telesford was onstage in the middle of a joke when she noticed blinking lights coming from the crowd. In an audio recording of her set that she shared with The Verge, Telesford can be heard addressing the man in the audience directly. “Are your glasses blinking?” she asks.  He responds that he’s recording her. “Oh, could you not?” she says. “That’s what they’re there for,” he says, defiantly. “I’m here to watch you, and you’re here to perform for me.” The audience member refuses to stop filming even after being asked to. Rather than argue back and forth, Telesford cuts her set short and walks offstage. “I was like, ‘I can’t do anything about it except get myself out of view of the camera on your face,’” she says of the exchange. “That’s all I can do.” At a comedy club or a more formal venue, audience members are typically told that recording isn’t allowed before a show starts. Events at bars, like the one Telesford was performing in, are typically more relaxed, she says. After the set, producers and hosts of the event spoke to the audience member and explained that comics are working on material for future opportunities where they can be paid for their performances, like television; having sets posted somewhere public could prevent performers from getting other distribution deals, since the material would no longer be exclusive. Going forward, the bar plans to announce at the beginning of performances that recording with Meta glasses is not allowed, Telesford says. “It’s definitely kind of tarnished every other interaction I’ve had,” Telesford says, even in front of audiences where the glasses aren’t present. “Every time I’ve been onstage since, it’s been a worry, a concern.” Being surreptitiously (or blatantly) recorded while at work isn’t just a problem for public-facing workers; it’s just as easy to imagine concerns that could arise if a coworker at your office starts wearing smart glasses, or if a medical professional wears them while providing care to a patient. Smart glasses reframe person-to-person interactions, creating a watchful technological mediary between two people. There’s a stark difference between having a casual, private conversation and the threat of everything you say or do being captured for limitless dissemination without your consent. [Image: Much of the pushback has focused on Meta glasses’ ability to invade privacy. Meta’s current smart glasses can only record for a few minutes, but it has ambitions to make the tech even more integrated into daily life. The company is reportedly developing smart glasses that record all the time, continuously pulling in data from audio and photos that the wearer could ask Meta AI about. What’s more, with the “super sensing” mode, the LED indicator light would not be on except when the wearer is actively taking photos and videos that are saved. The number of routine encounters that are recorded, saved, processed, and accessed later could skyrocket, effectively quantifying even the most mundane or private parts of our lives. Hartzog, the law professor, says, “This is just another way for employees who already have less power in their roles to be further marginalized and dissected, and is part of a larger story about the way in which being an employee means taking on increased suffering as part of the job.”

articles.title: US says hackers are targeting vulnerable water systems with the help of AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Hackers are targeting internet-connected Siemens controllers used in water facilities around the United States.
articles.body:
Amidst a spate of ongoing cyberattacks targeting water systems across the country, the U.S. government’s security agencies are warning that hackers are actively breaking into Siemens devices used in critical infrastructure.

U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and the National Security Agency, among others, said on Wednesday that hackers are targeting “all” Siemens S7 programmable logic controllers, which are devices used for controlling automated physical processes in energy, water systems, manufacturing, and agriculture.

CISA said the attacks are part of broader activity targeting water supply and wastewater systems around the United States. The agency said that the disruption could result in downtime, safety incidents, or equipment damage to critical infrastructure that relies on these devices.

The agencies said the hackers are using AI to generate exploit scripts that rely on publicly available information to find and exploit vulnerable programmable logic controllers that are running out-of-date software or are otherwise poorly secured.

CISA has long warned owners of critical infrastructure to keep these devices disconnected from the internet, and officials have acknowledged that rural communities are often the most affected because these systems service large geographic areas.

An incident response professional who works with critical infrastructure told TechCrunch that it was noteworthy that the hackers are using AI to identify and target vulnerable programmable logic controllers, as well as to understand how these devices work. But he cautioned that these devices are already highly vulnerable to begin with.

This is the latest warning from CISA following a series of cyberattacks by suspected Iranian hackers targeting U.S. water suppliers and wastewater providers in recent months. CISA said the attacks have escalated since Iranian hackers first targeted internet-connected systems used in critical infrastructure.

Officials across the U.S. have reported intrusions at water facilities in Minnesota and Michigan , as well as Arkansas , Georgia , and New Jersey .

articles.title: AI data giant Alation confirms cyberattack
articles.summary: The data search and AI giant confirmed unauthorized access to its systems during an incident on Tuesday, and said it was investigating the breach.
articles.body:
Days after reporting an incident affecting a number of its customers, enterprise data giant Alation on Thursday confirmed a cyberattack.

Alation makes data software that its enterprise customers use to search for files and data using natural language queries. In recent years, the company has expanded into AI , allowing customers to turn large amounts of messy data into usable content. The company says it services more than 500 global companies, including around half of the Fortune 1000 largest companies in the United States.

When reached by TechCrunch about the incident, the company said it was investigating.

“Alation recently identified an isolated incident involving unauthorized activity in one of its systems,” the company said in a statement provided to TechCrunch by an external representative, Stephen Russell. “We are conducting a thorough investigation of what occurred and we will provide additional information as appropriate.”

Alation did not specify the nature of the cyberattack, mention the root cause of the incident, or say how many customers are affected. The company did not say if it had alerted its customers to the incident or what defensive actions, if any, they should take following the intrusion.

On Tuesday, Alation reported an unspecified incident that resulted in “degraded availability” for some of its customers. The company said it had resolved the incident within an hour.

Much of the company’s systems are hosted on Amazon Web Services. It’s not immediately clear if any data was stolen or exfiltrated during the incident.

This is the latest cybersecurity incident in recent weeks to affect a large-scale technology giant, as hackers increasingly target companies that store large amounts of sensitive or proprietary information for their corporate customers.

Earlier this month, several companies reported data thefts following a breach at European shipping giant Ceva Logistics . Hackers are also said to be targeting financial firms and private equity giants in recent weeks.

articles.title: Frozen blueberries recall categorized under FDA’s highest Class I risk level
articles.summary: The recalled blueberries had been shipped to stores in eight states.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) – A recall of frozen blueberries sold at Publix supermarkets has been categorized under the most severe risk level by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

The recall was first initiated in early July by Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. of Chile, following a dozen reports of consumers experiencing E. coli-linked digestive illnesses, Publix previously announced. In response, Publix recalled 10-ounce packages of its private-label Frozen GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries. Publix later expanded the recall to include certain 48-ounce packages of the blueberries “out of an abundance of caution,” as well.

The recalled Frozen GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries had been shipped to stores in all eight states where Publix operates : Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia.

Packages from the affected lot can identify the recalled blueberries can be identified by their size (10 ounces) and best-by date of Feb. 9, 2028, according to the FDA’s latest enforcement report.

Publix says customers “are reminded not to consume them, and the product(s) should be discarded or returned to Publix for a full refund.”

This past Tuesday, the FDA ultimately issued a “Class I” categorization for the blueberry recall. The FDA says a Class 1 recall is “a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.”

The FDA has previously explained, however, that it often categorizes a recall well after the initiating firm makes the recall announcement, so classifications should not necessarily be viewed “as an expansion or change” to the firm’s initial recall.

The FDA urges any consumers who had eaten the recalled blueberries to contact a healthcare provider if they experience symptoms of possible E. coli infection.

E. coli “can cause bad stomach cramps, bloody loose stools and vomiting, called diarrheal infection,” according to the Mayo Clinic . Young children and older adults are at the highest risk of developing serious health complications from it.

Consumers can contact Publix at (800) 242-1227 with questions.

Nexstar’s Michael Bartiromo contributed to this report.

articles.title: Salmonella infections climb to 431 cases across multiple states: CDC
articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Wednesday that the salmonella outbreak linked to consumption of certain kinds of jalapeno peppers has grown to 431 cases across 32 states. The number includes 57 hospitalizations and no reported deaths as of Wednesday. It is up from 345 cases in 27 states reported in early…
articles.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Wednesday that the salmonella outbreak linked to consumption of certain kinds of jalapeno peppers has grown to 431 cases across 32 states.

The number includes 57 hospitalizations and no reported deaths as of Wednesday. It is up from 345 cases in 27 states reported in early August. The CDC estimates the number could be higher as many people recover from salmonella without receiving medical care or being tested.

The outbreak is believed to have begun between June 19 and Aug. 2 in Sinaloa, Mexico, and traceback data from the CDC suggests the contaminated product was distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors.

Salmonella is a common foodborne illness with symptoms that can include ​diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps. The CDC estimates this can start between six hours and six days after infection and can last four to seven days.

The states with the highest concentration of cases are Minnesota and Colorado, which account for more than 50 percent of the cases reported.

State and local health officials found 91 percent of the individuals who were interviewed ate at a Mexican-style restaurant including Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba . Chipotle switched its supplier while Qdoba stopped serving jalapeno peppers altogether.

Whole Foods was the latest company to issue a recall on Aug. 12 for products that include the peppers such as guacamole, pico de gallo, salsa and condiments. NatureBest and HEB salsas, soup mix and other products were also voluntarily recalled on Aug. 8.

Taylor Farms previously issued its own recall for the produce, and officials are still investigating the company for potential links to the ongoing cyclospora outbreak. The Food and Drug Administration reports seven active investigations into cyclospora outbreaks, with nearly 15,000 cases of domestically acquired cyclosporiasis confirmed in the U.S. since May this year.

The CDC ⁠estimates ​salmonella causes around 1.35 ​million infections in the United States every year.

articles.title: Almanacs release predictions for fall, winter – but can you trust them?
articles.summary: Sure, it’s only August, but wouldn’t you like to know what kind of weather to expect in the coming months?
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — It’s that time of year again. Sunsets are creeping earlier , mornings are starting to feel crisp. A quick look at the calendar shows the autumnal equinox is only about a month away.

Which means, of course, that the almanacs have released their look-ahead forecasts.

The Old Farmer’s Almanac and the Farmers’ Almanac are separate periodicals. In addition to the extended forecasts, you will also find gardening tips and skywatching advice.

Last month, the Old Farmer’s Almanac put out its fall forecast, predicting a “warmer than average” fall, with a “cool, wet” outlook in the Pacific Northwest and northern New England. Much of the Plains and Rocky Mountains could see a warm and dry fall, as could some states in the central Gulf region, while the Midwest, Ohio Valley and the East Coast may experience a cool and dry fall.

If that sounds familiar, it’s because it isn’t that much unlike the forecast the Old Farmer’s Almanac put out last year .

Looking even further ahead, the Farmers’ Almanac recently released its winter weather predictions , calling for “snow, sleet and surprises.”

Generally, it forecasts that all of the U.S. could see precipitation, whether it’s “snowy” in the upper Plains and Midwest, “wet” across the Gulf and southern East Coast, “wetter” in the South or “coastal storms” in New England.

That’s slightly different from last year’s forecast:

Regardless of how alike or unlike these forecasts are to previous predictions, how accurate can they actually be?

“There are those who believe [them] and those who don’t,” meteorologist Rich Segal, who recently retired from Nexstar’s KXAN, previously explained.

Both publications claim to be 80% accurate with their long-range forecasts, which are fueled by their own secret formulas, though research shows only about half of the forecasts produced by the Farmers’ Almanac were correct.

The Old Farmer’s Almanac says its formula , created in 1792, considers solar science, climatology and meteorology. They compare “solar patterns and historical weather conditions with current solar activity.”

The Farmers’ Almanac’s formula , established in 1818, has evolved through the years. One of its main factors is the moon’s influence, as well as a comparison between previous weather patterns and current conditions.

However, the far-ahead planning that both publications employ causes pause for some.

“It’s more like a crapshoot of trusting something that far into the future since there are times the forecast is blown in the first 24 hours,” Segal explained.

You won’t see a winter weather forecast from the National Weather Service until mid-October, for example. Even that outlook is subject to change, and if it were released any earlier, its reliability would likely decline, Jon Gottschalck, Operational Prediction Branch Chief at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, told Nexstar.

Those outlooks also won’t predict specific events, such as major winter storms.

“It’s just not possible to do that,” Gottschalck said.

There are temperature and precipitation outlooks available for early fall via NOAA. But these are based on probability. For example, the upper Pacific Northwest is favored to see a warmer-than-average September, October and November. The southern Midwest and Ohio Valley, meanwhile, have an equal chance of a warmer or cooler fall.

NOAA, the Farmer’s Almanac and the Old Farmer’s Almanac do review some of the same factors.

That includes what could become the strongest El Niño pattern we’ve seen since 1950 .

Last week, national forecasters said the odds of this year’s El Niño reaching the highest strength level – often called a “super” El Niño – are now higher than 90%. The peak could come between October and December, which may continue to support the quiet hurricane season we’ve seen in the Atlantic and influence our winter.

Under a typical El Niño , the northern U.S. and into the Ohio Valley usually see a warmer, drier weather pattern. The southern portion of the country, meanwhile, may have a wetter winter with more rain and snow. However, the exact line that separates these different weather outlooks varies from year to year.

How El Niño actually impacts our winter remains to be seen.

So can you trust the almanac predictions? Ultimately, it’s up to you.

“It has its value to those who believe in it and subscribe as such,” Segal said. NOAA will have an outlook for the winter months — December, January, and February — in mid-October. Its current three-month outlook is for August, September and October.

“While no forecast can claim perfect accuracy, our predictions have proven useful for generations of planners and outdoor enthusiasts,” Sandi Duncan, the editor of the Farmers’ Almanac, told Nexstar last year. “We continuously refine our method but acknowledge that Mother Nature always has the final say.”

Nexstar’s Alix Martichoux contributed to this report.

articles.title: GOP senator places hold on Trump nominees over wetlands policy
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) is placing a hold on all future Trump nominees over the administration’s approach to wetlands. In a statement shared with The Hill, Cramer expressed disappointment that the administration is leaving a Biden-era wetland policy in place for the time being — and indicated that he would not advance the president’s…
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) is placing a hold on all future Trump nominees over the administration’s approach to wetlands.

In a statement shared with The Hill, Cramer expressed disappointment that the administration is leaving a Biden-era wetland policy in place for the time being — and indicated that he would not advance the president’s nominees as a result.

“The blind defense of a Biden rule favored by environmental extremists at the expense of farmers confounds me, particularly at a time when our ag producers are hurting so badly,” he said.

“My farmers are furious and so am I. There won’t be another nominee confirmed until something changes,” he said.

The holds were first reported by E&E News .

Holds can slow the process of confirming nominees, requiring the Senate to spend hours debating them and taking additional votes for each nominee.

While they don’t necessarily prevent confirmation if a nominee can still reach a majority, in large quantities they can cause a significant setback, as seen when Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) put holds on hundreds of military promotions in 2023.

The Senate is currently in recess and is not actively advancing nominations, but it could seek to push more Trump appointees through this fall while Republicans are still certain to hold a majority.

Cramer’s hold comes as the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) decided not to move forward with changes to a Biden-era policy that sought to prevent the draining of wetlands that were protected under conservation easements — thereby protecting duck habitat.

Earlier this year, the agency said it would request information about whether to reconsider how the Biden-era rule calculates acceptable drain placement near wetlands.

In deciding not to move forward, FWS said in a post on the social platform X that it “is dedicated to protecting both the wetland easements purchased by the FWS that are necessary to protect our conservation heritage as well as the private landowners’ use of their lands outside the easement boundaries.”

“At this time, no further action is planned as we review the information received,” it said.

The Hill has reached out to FWS and the Interior Department for comment.

The issue is one that divides two constituencies that often lean Republican: hunters and farmers.

Hunters have supported the Biden-era rule, saying they want the best possible breeding habitat for ducks so they can hunt them in the future.

“Strong duck populations and liberal hunting opportunities depend upon maintaining the habitat conditions necessary for successful nesting and recruitment,” said a public comment from Illinois Ducks Unlimited.

On the other hand, opponents argue that the rule puts too many restrictions on farmers, who may want to put a drain on their lands.

“By establishing expansive, formula-driven setback requirements, the rule effectively extended federal control well beyond the boundaries of the easements themselves. What was sold to landowners as protection of specific wetland features became, in practice, a significant restriction on the productive use of additional adjacent private land, without additional compensation,” said a comment from the North Dakota Farm Bureau.

images.caption: Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) addresses reporters before the weekly Senate Republican policy luncheon on July 30, 2024.

articles.title: NOAA releases fall weather predictions for all 50 states as El Niño grows stronger
articles.summary: Fall is just around the corner, but summer weather may be sticking around a little while longer.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Fall is just around the corner, but summer weather may be sticking around a little while longer. A seasonal outlook released by national forecasters on Thursday shows most of the country is expected to see warmer-than-average weather over the next three months.

The long-range forecast, produced by NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, shows all but a few states leaning toward hotter-than-normal temperatures between September and November. The Pacific Northwest is most likely to see above-average weather, according to the map.

The future is murkier for a handful of states shown in white on the map below. Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Ohio, Tennessee and West Virginia have about equal chances of seeing a warm fall, a cool fall and an average fall.

When it comes to precipitation, even more states are seeing a toss-up situation.

The Southwest and Southeast are more likely to see above-average rain, while the Northeast and Pacific Northwest are more likely to be dry.

The forecast isn’t very clear for everyone else. Most states have equal chances of below-average, above-average or average precipitation between now and November.

Hawaii, which isn’t shown on the maps above, has a different outlook. Oahu, Maui, Kauai and the Big Island are most likely to see above-normal temperatures this fall, before shifting to a cooler winter season in early 2027. Below-normal precipitation is increasingly likely for all of Hawaii starting in October, the Climate Prediction Center said.

Last Thursday , national forecasters said the odds that the 2026-2027 El Niño will reach the highest strength level — often called a “super” El Niño — are now higher than 90%.

The climate phenomenon has slowly gained steam since it officially started earlier this summer, and is expected to reach maximum strength in late fall or early winter. That’s when it would have the strongest chokehold on our weather patterns.

Typically, El Niño produces warmer, dry weather up north and in the Ohio Valley. Meanwhile, the southern half of the country usually gets a wetter winter, with more rain and snow. The exact dividing line moves year to year, depending on the position of the jet stream.

Some early signs of those patterns can be seen in the fall weather forecasts released Thursday, especially in the warm, dry Pacific Northwest, and the wetter southern states.

Other impacts of El Niño on fall weather include suppressing hurricane activity in the Atlantic and contributing to more high-tide flooding on the West Coast.

articles.title: Senate Dems press Hegseth for answers on Stars and Stripes independence
articles.summary: A trio of Senate Democrats is expressing concern over the Pentagon’s involvement in the operations of Stars and Stripes, defending the publication’s independence in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday. Their inquiry follows an announcement this week that the military newspaper’s longtime publisher, Max Lederer, will be retiring after the Pentagon appointed…
articles.body:
A trio of Senate Democrats is expressing concern over the Pentagon’s involvement in the operations of Stars and Stripes, defending the publication’s independence in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday.

Their inquiry follows an announcement this week that the military newspaper’s longtime publisher, Max Lederer, will be retiring after the Pentagon appointed an active-duty Navy captain to a top role at the paper without consulting him.

Lederer said his decision to step down stemmed from “fundamental” differences between his and the department’s visions for the paper. The publisher will depart his role at the end of next month.

The senators wrote in their Thursday letter that the appointment of William Urban, an active-duty Navy captain and public affairs officer, as Lederer’s deputy “raises serious questions” about the paper’s independence.

“Mr. Lederer’s abrupt departure only heightens those concerns, particularly as the Department determines who will assume leadership of Stars and Stripes,” they said.

The letter was signed by Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) and Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), who all sit on the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The lawmakers requested that the Defense secretary provide them with a “detailed explanation” of Urban’s appointment by Aug. 28.

The Hill has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

“Please also explain what safeguards the Department has put in place to ensure that this officer, or any other Department official, cannot direct, influence, review, or interfere with Stars and Stripes’ editorial decisions or coverage,” they added.

This is the latest development in the Pentagon’s efforts to reshape the military newspaper’s coverage. In a March memo , the Defense Department outlined new guidelines for Stars and Stripes, including a requirement that its content be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.”

Additionally, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January that the Pentagon would “refocus” the outlet away from “woke distractions that siphon morale.”

Lederer told Stars and Stripes following his resignation announcement that he was not aligned with “the pace and the direction” of the department’s goals for the outlet.

“I think the right step is for me to step down, get out of the way, and let different leadership step in and continue to make this the great organization that it is, even better,” he said.

images.caption: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth leaves a meeting with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 4, 2026.

articles.title: Invited media, military members held at gunpoint by Space Force security
articles.summary: Five journalists and the two military members escorting them to an event at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., this week were briefly detained at gunpoint by security police who believed they were gate crashers, according to the local media affected. The Monday incident happened ahead of an invitation-only groundbreaking for a new training facility for…
articles.body:
Five journalists and the two military members escorting them to an event at Vandenberg Space Force Base , Calif., this week were briefly detained at gunpoint by security police who believed they were gate crashers, according to the local media affected.

The Monday incident happened ahead of an invitation-only groundbreaking for a new training facility for missile operators. Reporters for KEYT, Noozhawk, KSBY and the Santa Maria Times were let onto the base and began to follow a military escort vehicle — a government minivan with uniformed public affairs staff — but were quickly stopped and ordered out of their vehicles at gunpoint with their hands up, KEYT reported .

The incident occurred due to at least one security force member raising an alert of “gate runners,” prompting the reporters’ temporary detainment and metal barricades to be raised, according to Noozhawk .

The journalists were told to sit on the curb nearby while the two military member escorts were handcuffed and placed in base vehicles, according to the outlet.

The incident lasted more than 30 minutes, causing the media members to miss the ceremony they were invited to cover. All reporters were let go without further action.

Space Launch Delta 30 ‘s public affairs office labeled the incident as a “breakdown in communication.”

“Vandenberg Space Force Base is experiencing an increased number of unauthorized entry attempts,” according to a statement to the local outlets. “Every potential unauthorized presence must be treated as a legitimate threat until proven otherwise.”

“While we recognize this may have been unsettling, the security of the base and its personnel is our priority,” they added.

Tom Bolton, Noozhawk’s editor-in-chief, said Wednesday that while his organization respects the military’s need to provide security for the base, “clearly what occurred was unfortunate and unnecessary, and potentially dangerous, as firearms were drawn.”

He added that it “appears some members of the Vandenberg security team are seriously in need of additional training,” and called the incident “a failure on multiple levels, and the base owes apologies to the affected journalists. The military’s response certainly was lacking.”

articles.title: FCC officially decides gigabit speeds are too good for you
articles.summary: Why is the government lowering the nation’s ambition?
articles.body: Another day, another sad thing to report about our compromised Federal Communications Commission. Chairman Brendan Carr has followed through on his 2025 threat to kill long-term broadband speed goals established during the Biden administration, which aimed for eventually getting us to gigabit download and half-gigabit upload speeds. How dare we dream of spreading great download and upload speeds across the country! It’s wild that 13 years after Comcast said Americans don’t need gigabit internet we’re somehow back in this conversation. Especially since the private sector has delivered, albeit unevenly, on super high speeds in certain areas; For example, the apartment I’m about to move into offers 5 gigabit synchronous internet speed which will require a new PCIe network card to handle. Those speeds are ludicrous, but why are we not aiming for the moon across the country? It took years for the FCC to finally admit publicly that the outdated 25Mbps definition of “broadband” speed sucked. Remember Ajit Pai, the guy with the giant Reese’s mug who killed net neutrality? He once said we didn’t need more than that. (The standard was raised from 25/3 to 100/20 in 2024.) Pai’s successor Brendan Carr — who is far worse in almost every category — is repeating the same stuff but in an even more cynical way. Here’s part of what the FCC says about its decision to abandon the gigabit speed goal: > At present, it is impossible to predict long-term technological developments and the evolution of consumer preferences. This is one of the least-impossible things to predict. Who would possibly choose for things to be slower if they could be faster? This is peak regulatory arrogance from an administration that is generally not shy about lying through its teeth to the public. But, no worries. The abandonment of the gigabit goal is wrapped inside a broader broadband report that claims everything is just fine! The FCC says speeds are up, competition is up, and prices are down. Too bad, as Ars Technica notes, that some of these insights are sourced from industry lobby groups and no adverse research from advocacy groups. Why is the FCC doing this? Who knows, but here’s a solid guess: the FCC has been further captured by industry interests that would love for their pet projects (like satellite internet) not to look bad when compared to high standards. Just how much has the FCC been captured? Incidentally, The Guardian reported just today that Brendan Carr has been exceptionally cozy with the White House and right-wing media. It’s an easy bet to make that killing the broadband goal has nothing to do with public interests.

articles.title: New study finds link between sugary drinks and stomach cancer
articles.summary: People who consume one or more sugary drinks a day are more than two times at risk for stomach cancer.
articles.body:
(NewsNation) — A new study by Mass General Bingham points to a link between consumption of sugary drinks and gastric (stomach) cancer.

The study categorized sugary drinks as lemonade, punch, sport drinks and carbonated beverages. The study looked at 112,284 people from the Nurses’ Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-Up.

It followed participants over decades, with 278 eventually developing stomach cancer.

The results showed participants who consumed one sugary drink per day were over two times more likely to develop stomach cancer than those who consumed less than one per month.

Sugary drinks had previously been linked to other forms of cancer; breast, liver and colorectum.

According to CDC data , 63 percent of adults consume one or more sugary drinks per day. Stomach cancer is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S.

The study notes limitations and that the cancer diagnosis could have been due to other factors such as family history. Further research is needed in order to officially establish causality.

articles.title: Aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln after lengthy deployment
articles.summary: The USS George Washington aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East theater this week to provide relief for the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose lengthy deployment has drawn scrutiny over reports of worsening sailors’ mental health and supply shortages while supporting the U.S. war against Iran. The U.S. military confirmed on Thursday that the USS George…
articles.body:
The USS George Washington aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East theater this week to provide relief for the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose lengthy deployment has drawn scrutiny over reports of worsening sailors’ mental health and supply shortages while supporting the U.S. war against Iran.

The U.S. military confirmed on Thursday that the USS George Washington, which came from U.S. Pacific Command (Pacom), got to the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) area of responsibility on Wednesday. This leaves the U.S. without a carrier strike group in Asia.

The USS George Washington, which is based in Japan, joins the USS George H.W. Bush, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, as the second aircraft carrier in the Middle East, where the U.S. Navy is enforcing a blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

After news reports citing a shortage of food and hygiene products, along with poor mental health of sailors amid a record deployment that began in late November, the USS Abraham Lincoln will be returning home to the U.S.

Reports have prompted Democratic lawmakers to press the Navy and Pentagon for answers about the conditions on board the aircraft carrier, conditions that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said were “completely misrepresented.”

Over the weekend, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of Centcom, visited the crew at the Lincoln, praising the service members for delivering a performance for the “ages, and now you are going home.”

“Recent media reporting has portrayed varying perspectives on operational tempo, crew morale and the realities facing our deployed forces. What I found aboard the Lincoln is that many elements of those stories are old news,” Cooper wrote in an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal, which was published Sunday.

“I chatted with junior enlisted personnel and junior officers in small groups,” Cooper said. “Issues related to food, hot water and other concerns raised months ago were addressed by leadership and resolved.”

articles.title: Someone targeted security researchers using a fake crypto conference as a lure | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A hacker pretending to work for a leading cryptocurrency news website targeted several cybersecurity professionals using Google Docs as a way to deliver malware.
articles.body:
If you are a malicious hacker, cybersecurity professionals may very well be the worst people in the world to try to hack, as there is a very good chance they are going to catch you.

A person pretending to work for a leading crypto news site targeted several cybersecurity professionals around the time of the Black Hat and Def Con hacking conferences earlier this month. The hacker approached attendees on the social media site X, both via public replies and DMs, and then leveraged Google Docs in an attempt to trick the targets into installing malware, according to researchers.

On Wednesday, security firm Huntress published a blog post detailing the hacking campaign, which targeted one of its researchers, who pretended to go along with it to learn what the hacker was trying to do.

In broken English, the hacker asked the researcher if they had plans to attend a conference next, and then mentioned a conference allegedly organized by the crypto news website, according to a screenshot of the conversation.

After that, the hacker shared a legitimate Google Doc that looked like it was a planning document for the fake conference. The document displayed a sidebar designed to make the target think it was encrypted. The goal was to first trick the target into entering a fake decryption key provided by the hacker. That was the first step in a process that would lead to the installation of malware for macOS and Windows, depending on the operating system used by the target, according to Huntress.

To make the sidebar appear real, the hacker used Google App Script , a platform that allows developers to customize the user interface of Google Docs with menus and sidebars, for example.

The hacker tried to trick Huntress’ researcher into installing an infostealer for Apple computers; a remote desktop viewing tool repurposed as malware for Windows; and a fake installer for the cryptocurrency wallet Ledger.

The person behind the account identified by Huntress researchers as the hacker did not respond when TechCrunch sent them a private message on X.

Hackers of all kinds — whether they are unknown government hackers using advanced spyware or North Korean government hackers using fake Twitter profiles — have targeted cybersecurity professionals before. What made this campaign a bit more believable was the use of a legitimate Google Doc and Google feature.

Google did not immediately respond when TechCrunch reached out asking if the company had seen this or similar hacking campaigns.

articles.title: CFTC chair vows to ‘move swiftly’ on crypto rules if Congress fails to pass legislation
articles.summary: The head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) vowed Thursday to “move swiftly” on establishing rules for the cryptocurrency market if Congress fails to pass legislation on the matter this year. CFTC Chair Michael Selig said at a meeting with crypto and prediction market executives that the agency stands “ready to begin immediately implementing…
articles.body:
The head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) vowed Thursday to “move swiftly” on establishing rules for the cryptocurrency market if Congress fails to pass legislation on the matter this year.

CFTC Chair Michael Selig said at a meeting with crypto and prediction market executives that the agency stands “ready to begin immediately implementing the bill,” known as the Clarity Act, if passed.

However, he added, “If Clarity continues to stall because of Democrat obstruction, the CFTC will utilize its existing authorities to begin establishing a regime for crypto asset markets. We owe it to the American people to do so.”

“We will heed President Trump’s call to codify a future-proof digital asset market structure that cannot be undone by the crypto haters,” Selig continued.

The Clarity Act aims to create a regulatory framework for the industry by splitting oversight between the CFTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Senate Republicans and crypto-friendly Democrats have been negotiating on the bill for nearly a year, but several key sticking points remain. Most notably, Democrats are pushing for stronger ethics restrictions.

Despite a push to pass the legislation by the August recess, Senate GOP leaders ultimately punted a vote to mid-September, dimming the measure’s prospects of passing this year.

Selig said Tuesday that he has directed his staff to “begin exploring rules to codify a CFTC market structure for crypto assets using the agency’s existing authorities.”

Under such rules, crypto exchanges would be designated by the CFTC as crypto asset markets and permitted to offer trading, Selig said. He also noted his staff is looking into establishing ways for developers to “offer their protocols in a legal and compliant manner.”

“We’re going to give Clarity its breathing room for a vote, but if the Democrats cannot support a bipartisan work product which reflects compromises from both sides of the aisle and ultimately send a fair version of the bill to the president’s desk, then rest assured, I will direct CFTC staff to move swiftly to propose these rules for the industry,” he added.

articles.title: Americans’ drinking remains at record low: Poll
articles.summary: Americans’ drinking remains at historically low levels with a survey released Thursday reporting the lowest levels of alcohol consumption among Americans in its history, dating back to 1939. A new Gallup survey found the share of Americans who consume alcohol held at 54 percent for the second consecutive year. Self-reported drinking has been falling in…
articles.body:
Americans’ drinking remains at historically low levels with a survey released Thursday reporting the lowest levels of alcohol consumption among Americans in its history, dating back to 1939.

A new Gallup survey found the share of Americans who consume alcohol held at 54 percent for the second consecutive year. Self-reported drinking has been falling in recent years from 62 percent in 2023 to 58 percent in 2024 and 54 percent in 2025.

It found across most demographic groups that drinking had fallen from 2023 to 2026 — including among all age groups, white and nonwhite adults, and men and women. The only subgroup for which drinking did not decline was Americans who attended religious service weekly, which did not change at 48 percent.

Gallup also noted that 51 percent of American adult respondents said they believe drinking one to two alcoholic beverages per day is bad for one’s health, while 40 percent said it makes no difference.

Guidance surrounding alcohol consumption has remained a debated topic under the Trump administration as it shifted previous guidelines.

At the beginning of the year, the 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA) were announced and notably removed the previous recommendation to limit alcohol consumption to one drink or fewer daily for women and two drinks or fewer for men.

Instead the new guidance advised: “Consume less alcohol for better health.”

Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, followed up this guidance, saying drinking should usually be done in moderation and socially. “The implication is don’t have it for breakfast,” he said.

Researchers who have been studying the effects of drinking since 2022 were informed by the Trump administration in 2025 that it did not plan to publish their results.

The study, released in June in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs , found no benefits to moderate levels of drinking. It recommended that adults should limit themselves to one drink or less per day and stated these findings should have informed the latest DGA.

The Gallup survey took place July 1-19 among a random sample of 1,200 adults. The margin of sampling error is 4 percentage points.
